lead: A two-port network is a circuit seen only through two pairs of terminals: one pair where the signal goes in and one pair where it comes out. Each pair is a port, so the current that enters one terminal of the pair leaves by the other. The inside is hidden, and the outside is described by four quantities, V₁, I₁, V₂ and I₂, linked by two equations. Transistor models, filters, transformers and transmission lines are all handled this way, because only their input and output behaviour matters to the rest of the circuit.
prereq: You need Kirchhoff's laws, series and parallel resistance, and the voltage and current division rules.

blocks.text: A terminal is a point where an outside wire connects. A port is a pair of terminals with one condition: the current entering one terminal equals the current leaving the other. Then the pair carries one voltage (across it) and one current (through it). This is called the port condition.

A one-port has one such pair; a resistor, or any network judged by its input impedance alone, is a one-port. A two-port has two pairs, labelled 1–1′ (port 1, the input) and 2–2′ (port 2, the output). A multi-port has three or more ports, such as a three-winding transformer. Some syllabi call a two-port a four-terminal network or a quadripole.

Many two-ports have only three terminals, because terminals 1′ and 2′ are the same wire. A T network and a transistor in common-emitter use are examples: the common terminal returns I₁ from port 1 and I₂ from port 2, so both port conditions still hold. The port condition fails only when an outside path joins the two ports, for example a wire from terminal 1 to terminal 2′ in another part of the circuit; then a terminal pair no longer carries equal and opposite currents and the two-port description breaks.

To describe a two-port by four fixed constants it must be linear (no powers or products of the port variables), contain no independent sources, and start with zero stored energy in its inductors and capacitors. Dependent sources are allowed; they are how a transistor model gets its gain.

This book uses the convention found in most textbooks. V₁ is the voltage of terminal 1 with respect to 1′, and I₁ is the current entering terminal 1. V₂ is the voltage of terminal 2 with respect to 2′, and I₂ is the current entering terminal 2. Both currents are drawn into the network. The arrows define the positive direction; the real current may flow the other way, and then the value is negative.
With both currents entering, the power entering the two-port from outside is

blocks.where: where P in watts is positive when the network absorbs power and negative when it delivers power to the outside (a passive network can never give P < 0).

blocks.text: A load Z<sub>L</sub> at port 2 carries the current that leaves terminal 2, which is −I₂. Ohm's law on the load therefore reads V₂ = −I₂Z<sub>L</sub>. This one minus sign appears in every terminated two-port calculation of this unit.

A linear two-port with no internal sources fixes two linear relations among V₁, I₁, V₂ and I₂. So only two of the four are free: pick any two as the inputs and the network decides the other two. Each choice of the free pair gives one parameter set of four constants:

Six ways of choosing two variables out of four give six sets. They describe the same box, so any one can be found from another by algebra; see conversions between parameter sets. When a source and a load are connected, the outside circuit adds two more equations (one at each port), and the four port variables become definite numbers, as the worked example shows.

figure.caption: The T network as a two-port between a 12 V source and a 1 Ω load. Both arrows I₁ and I₂ point into the network; the real load current leaves terminal 2, so I₂ = −1.5 A and V₂ = −I₂ × 1 Ω = 1.5 V.

spec.aria: A T network of 2, 3 and 4 ohms inside a dashed box with terminals 1, 1 prime, 2, 2 prime. A 12 volt source drives port 1 with I1 = 3 A entering; a 1 ohm load at port 2 carries 1.5 A out, so I2 entering is minus 1.5 A and V2 is 1.5 V.

examples.question: A T network has a series arm Z₁ = 2 Ω from terminal 1 to a centre node, a series arm Z₂ = 3 Ω from the centre node to terminal 2, and a shunt arm Z₃ = 4 Ω from the centre node to the common terminal 1′–2′. A 12 V source is connected at port 1 and a 1 Ω load at port 2. Find V₁, I₁, V₂ and I₂ with the standard convention, and the power entering the two-port. Check the power by adding the resistor losses.
steps: Seen from the centre node, the branch towards port 2 is Z₂ + Z<sub>L</sub> = 3 + 1 = 4 Ω. It is in parallel with Z₃ = 4 Ω: 4 × 4/(4 + 4) = 2 Ω.
Input resistance: R<sub>in</sub> = Z₁ + 2 = 2 + 2 = 4 Ω. The source fixes V₁ = 12 V, so I₁ = 12/4 = 3 A (entering terminal 1, so positive).
Centre-node voltage: 12 − 3 × 2 = 6 V. The current down Z₃ is 6/4 = 1.5 A; the current towards the load is 6/4 = 1.5 A. KCL at the centre: 3 = 1.5 + 1.5 ✓.
The load current 1.5 A leaves terminal 2, so V₂ = 1.5 × 1 = 1.5 V and I₂ = −1.5 A (it enters terminal 2 as −1.5 A). Check V₂ = −I₂Z<sub>L</sub> = −(−1.5)(1) = 1.5 V ✓.
Power entering the two-port: P = V₁I₁ + V₂I₂ = 12 × 3 + 1.5 × (−1.5) = 36 − 2.25 = 33.75 W.

Resistor losses: Z₁: 3² × 2 = 18 W; Z₃: 1.5² × 4 = 9 W; Z₂: 1.5² × 3 = 6.75 W. Total 18 + 9 + 6.75 = 33.75 W ✓. The source gives 36 W; 33.75 W is lost inside and the 2.25 W that leaves port 2 heats the load.
examples.answer: V₁ = 12 V, I₁ = 3 A, V₂ = 1.5 V, I₂ = −1.5 A; the two-port absorbs P = 33.75 W, equal to its resistor losses, and passes 2.25 W to the load.
examples.check:
Z1,Z2,Z3,ZL,V1=2.0,3.0,4.0,1.0,12.0
par=Z3*(Z2+ZL)/(Z3+Z2+ZL)
Rin=Z1+par
I1=V1/Rin
Vc=V1-I1*Z1
IL=Vc/(Z2+ZL)
V2=IL*ZL
I2=-IL
P=V1*I1+V2*I2
loss=I1**2*Z1+(Vc/Z3)**2*Z3+IL**2*Z2
print(Rin,I1,V2,I2,P,loss,V2*IL)

traps: I₂ is defined entering port 2. The current a load draws is −I₂, so a load at port 2 gives V₂ = −I₂Z<sub>L</sub>, not +I₂Z<sub>L</sub>. In the worked example I₂ = −1.5 A, and writing +1.5 A makes P come out 38.25 W, more than the source gives.

A port is a pair of terminals with equal and opposite currents, not any two terminals. If an outside wire joins the input side to the output side, the pair condition fails and the parameters no longer describe the network.
A three-terminal network (common 1′–2′, as in a T network or a transistor) is a valid two-port. Its common terminal carries I₁ + I₂, and that is allowed.
The four port variables are not four free inputs. A linear two-port fixes two of them once the other two are chosen; a question that gives three port variables can be checked for consistency.
Fixed parameters need a linear network with no independent sources inside and zero initial stored energy. Dependent sources are fine.

quiz.q: Define a port and state the port condition.
quiz.a: A port is a pair of terminals through which one current enters and the same current leaves; it carries one voltage and one current. The port condition is that the current entering one terminal equals the current leaving the other.

quiz.q: Name the six two-port parameter sets and the free pair of variables of each.
quiz.a: Z (I₁, I₂), Y (V₁, V₂), h (I₁, V₂), g (V₁, I₂), ABCD (V₂, −I₂) and inverse transmission (V₁, −I₁).

quiz.q: Why does a linear two-port need exactly four parameters?
quiz.a: It has four port variables but fixes two linear relations among them, so two variables are free. Each of the two dependent variables is a linear combination of the two free ones, which takes two constants each: four in all.

quiz.q: A two-port has V₁ = 8 V, I₁ = 1.5 A, V₂ = −2 V and I₂ = 0.5 A, all with the standard convention. Find the power entering it.
quiz.a: P = V₁I₁ + V₂I₂ = 8 × 1.5 + (−2)(0.5) = 12 − 1 = 11 W. The two-port absorbs 11 W.

quiz.q: In the worked example the load is changed to 3 Ω. Find I₁, V₂ and I₂.
quiz.a: Z₂ + Z<sub>L</sub> = 6 Ω; 6 ∥ 4 = 2.4 Ω; R<sub>in</sub> = 4.4 Ω; I₁ = 12/4.4 = 2.727 A. Centre voltage 12 − 2 × 2.727 = 6.545 V; load current 6.545/6 = 1.091 A; V₂ = 3.273 V and I₂ = −1.091 A.

quiz.q: A student draws I₂ leaving port 2 and still writes P = V₁I₁ + V₂I₂. What goes wrong, and what is the correct expression with that arrow?
quiz.a: With the arrow leaving, the measured current is I₂′ = −I₂, so the power entering is V₁I₁ − V₂I₂′. Using +V₂I₂′ adds the load power instead of subtracting it: in the worked example it gives 38.25 W instead of 33.75 W.

quiz.q: Can a network that contains an independent source be described by four fixed parameters? Explain.
quiz.a: No. The source adds a constant term to each port equation (V₁ = z₁₁I₁ + z₁₂I₂ + V₀₁, for example), so the port variables are no longer proportional to the free pair. It needs four parameters plus two source terms, as in a Thévenin model at each port.

beyond: Not for the exam. At radio frequencies open and short circuits are hard to make, so two-ports are measured as scattering (S) parameters with a vector network analyser and stored in Touchstone (.s2p) files for simulators. Multi-port models with three or more ports describe couplers, three-winding transformers and the pins of a chip package. Search for “S parameters”, “Touchstone file” and “multiport network”.
